books.section: Topic 8.2 The Cold War from 1945 to 1980
Truman and the Beginning of the Cold War (1945-1953)

primary_sources: Harry S. Truman, address to a joint session of Congress, March 12, 1947 (House Document No. 171)

stimulus.text: The first page of a printed address by President Harry S. Truman to a joint session of Congress, March 12, 1947, headed 'Recommendation for Assistance to Greece and Turkey,' House Document No. 171. The page says the gravity of the situation requires the president's appearance, that the foreign policy and national security of the country are involved, and that Greece has suffered invasion, four years of cruel enemy occupation, and bitter internal strife.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool: first page of President Truman's address to Congress, March 12, 1947, House Document No. 171, public domain (U.S. government document)
stem: The document shown was the opening of the Truman Doctrine. Which of the following best describes the new direction in American foreign policy that this address announced?

options.text: The United States would return to the isolationism of the 1920s and avoid involvement in Europe's affairs.
options.misconception: Isolationism ended with the war; Truman's address committed America abroad, it did not pull America back.

options.text: The United States would rely on the United Nations alone to settle disputes with the Soviet Union.
options.misconception: The United Nations sponsored later actions such as Korea, but this 1947 address asked Congress for American aid.

options.text: The United States would give aid to free peoples resisting communist pressure, beginning with Greece and Turkey.
The United States would demand that Britain keep paying for the defense of Greece and Turkey.
options.misconception: Britain was withdrawing from Greece and Turkey, not being asked to keep paying.

rationales.A: Truman's address did the opposite of returning to isolationism. It committed the United States to a lasting role in Europe's defense, a break from the 1920s.
rationales.B: The United Nations is not mentioned on this page. Truman asked Congress, not the United Nations, to approve American aid.
rationales.C: The address asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey. Background from the books: Truman also stated the wider rule behind the request, that the United States would support free peoples resisting subjugation, and that rule became containment, the cornerstone of American foreign policy for decades.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Britain had already told Washington it could no longer afford to aid Greece and Turkey. That withdrawal is why Truman had to act.
rationales.general:
1. Read what Truman asks for. Money and help for Greece and Turkey, two countries under communist pressure.
2. Ask why America, not Britain. Background from the books: Britain could no longer afford to prop up Greece and Turkey, so the choice fell to Washington.
3. Ask what the aid means. It is not a one-time gift. It is a promise to stand behind any free people facing communist pressure.
4. Name the policy. Containment: holding the line against communist expansion wherever it appears.
Remember: the Truman Doctrine turned containment from an idea into an American promise.
